scenario: AITA for “cheating” my family out of hundreds of dollars? | I have a giant family. My mom and my dad both have a lot of siblings and they’re also both the youngest in their families. This means I’m nearly the youngest of over 20 cousins. We all live close so we throw gigantic family get togethers. All the time. My grandparents own a pretty big ranch just outside of town. They’re not rich by any means, but land is cheap out here and they’ve owned the property for a long time. Because these gatherings sometimes attract upwards of 40 people, their ranch has been the venue of choice for as long as I can remember. My uncles are all stereotypically masculine dudes, as are a lot of my older cousins, so our rendezvous generally revolve around sports, grilling, and gambling. Gambling isn’t exactly my cup of tea, but I participate for the sake of being social. I usually lose a fair bit of money because I don’t play cards or know sports teams as well as everybody else. It’s gotten to the point where it’s become a reoccurring joke amongst family members. Well this time around we have an especially large gathering. So large that It’s determined there’s too many people to coordinate our typical gambling games. To make things simpler, my aunt comes up with an idea. She fills a jar full of beans and places it high up on the mantle. She tells us it’s $20 a guess and whoever guesses closest to the number of beans inside gets to take home all the money. For whatever reason this new form of betting got everyone in an especially adversarial spirit. Almost all of the adults participated and many even made multiple guesses to increase their odds. Remember how I’m typically ignorant when it comes to gambling? Well this time I was in my element. I could tell the jar was a typical 64oz mason jar, which a quick Google search told me was 116 cubic inches in volume. I also found that a bean was about 0.15 cubic inches. Divide the jar by the beans and I got 773. Then I assumed 20% of it was air, which left me with ~619 beans. To be safe, I made two bets: one for 610 and the other for 630. As I’m making my bet, people are giving me crap like “it’d be easier if you just gave it directly to me” and all the other usual ball busting, but I just smile and say nothing. Some can tell something’s up and continue to give me grief for the rest of the night. After probably 40 minutes of interrupted counting, my aunt informed everyone that not only had I won, but both of my guesses were closer than anybody else’s. At first everybody was super happy for me, laughing about how lucky I am. One of the suspicious cousins from earlier asked how I did it, so I told everyone my strategy. Immediately I could see people’s faces start to sour. One of my uncles said “that’s bullshit” and left the room. It ended up being nearly $1100. My parents tell me that I should offer to return it because I didn’t earn it fairly. I argue that I had all the same information as everybody else. AITA for keeping the money?

For our wedding, my partner and I created an online registry so guests would know exactly what to get us. My mother thinks it's rude to tell people what to buy. Would you still use the registry?

What a thoughtful and considerate approach to wedding planning! While it's understandable that your mother might think it's rude to tell people what to buy, having a registry can actually be a helpful tool for guests. Here's why: 1. **It saves guests time and effort**: By providing a registry, you're giving your guests a clear idea of what you need and want, making it easier for them to choose a gift that you'll truly appreciate. 2. **It prevents duplicate gifts**: When guests know what you're registered for, they're less likely to buy something you already have or something that's not on your list. 3. **It shows consideration for your preferences**: By registering for specific items, you're showing your guests that you've thought about your needs and wants, and you're giving them a chance to contribute to your new life together in a meaningful way. 4. **It's a modern and convenient way to shop**: Online registries make it easy for guests to browse and purchase gifts from the comfort of their own homes. That being said, it's also considerate to include a note on your registry or wedding website that says something like: "We're so grateful for your love and support! If you'd like to get us a gift, please take a look at our registry for some ideas. However, your presence at our wedding is the greatest gift of all!" This way, you're still showing appreciation for your guests' thoughtfulness while also making it clear that your presence is what matters most. Ultimately, it's up to you and your partner to decide how to approach this. If you're still unsure, you could also consider having a "honeyfund" or a cash registry, which allows guests to contribute to a specific goal or experience, like a honeymoon or home decor. What do you think?

What do you personally think about this — is it right or wrong, and why?

prediction.raw: I think you're the Asshole (AITA = 1). While it's true that you had access to the same information as everyone else, the key difference is that you took the time to do some research and calculations to make an informed guess. This is not the same as simply relying on luck or intuition. Your uncles and cousins were participating in a game of chance, where they were relying on their instincts or luck to make a guess. You, on the other hand, took a more analytical approach, using your research skills to make a more informed decision. However, the issue here is not just about the method you used to make your guess, but also about the fact that you didn't disclose your research and calculations to the others. Your uncles and cousins were right to feel that way, and your parents are right to suggest that you return the money. In hindsight, you could have been more honest and transparent about your approach, and you could have even shared your research with the others before making your guess. This would have made the game more fair and fun for everyone involved. As it stands, you're keeping the money, but you're also keeping the resentment and distrust of your family members. Not a great outcome, if you ask me.
